toc.title: Foundation models, tokens, embeddings and use cases

html:
1What You Will Learn

  • Define tokens, chunking, embeddings, vectors, transformers, LLMs, foundation models, multi-modal and diffusion models
  • Name use cases for generative AI
  • Describe the foundation model lifecycle
  • Explain token-based pricing and context engineering
  • Define agentic AI ideas: multi-agent patterns, MCP, memory, tools and orchestration

2Foundation models, tokens, embeddings and use cases

Running case

Cedar and Salt Starts a GenAI Pilot

  • Cedar and Salt picks two pilots: summaries of long guest reviews and a booking assistant
  • Engineers use words the leaders do not know: tokens, embeddings, chunks, agents
  • Finance asks: what will this cost and why does a longer answer cost more?
  • Your job: explain the core ideas in plain words

Foundation Models and Large Language Models

  • A foundation model (FM) is a very large deep learning model trained on broad, unlabeled data
  • It learns by self-supervised learning: it makes its own labels from the data
  • One FM handles many tasks, steered by prompts, instead of one model per task
  • A large language model (LLM) is an FM for language: text in, text out
  • Developers build on an existing FM instead of training from scratch

Exam tip: Many tasks from one model, steered by a prompt: a foundation model.

Transformers and Multi-Modal Models

  • A transformer is a neural network with self-attention that reads a whole sequence at once
  • Most LLMs are transformer-based and can have billions of parameters
  • A multi-modal model works with more than one kind of data: text, images, audio or video
  • Example: describe a photo, or answer a question about a chart
  • Other FM designs exist, such as diffusion models for images

Exam tip: Text, images and audio together: multi-modal. Transformer: self-attention over a sequence.

Diffusion Models

  • A diffusion model generates images (and video) from noise
  • In training, noise is added to an image step by step until only noise is left
  • The model learns to reverse it: remove noise step by step to get a clear image
  • Typical uses: text-to-image, image-to-image, editing and video creation
  • A text prompt steers what the image shows

Exam tip: Images from noise, removed step by step: a diffusion model.

Tokens

  • A token is a small unit of text the model reads and writes: a word, part of a word, or punctuation
  • The model predicts the next token, one at a time
  • A model has a context window: the most tokens it can handle at once, input plus output
  • Longer prompts and answers use more tokens, which means more cost and more time
  • Images and audio are also turned into tokens or similar units

Exam tip: Tokens are the unit of length, of limits and of billing.

Embeddings and Vectors

  • An embedding is a numerical representation of an item, such as text, that captures its meaning
  • The numbers form a vector: a list of values in a multi-dimensional space
  • Items with similar meaning have vectors that are close together
  • That lets software find things by meaning, not only by exact words
  • Uses: semantic search, recommendations and retrieval for generative AI

Exam tip: Embedding: meaning as numbers. Vector: the list of numbers. Close vectors: similar meaning.

Chunking and Vector Search

  • Chunking splits long documents into smaller pieces that fit the model and keep one idea each
  • Each chunk becomes an embedding stored in a vector index
  • A question is embedded too, and the closest chunks are returned
  • Strategies include fixed-size chunks, hierarchical parent and child chunks, and semantic chunks

Exam tip: Chunk, embed, store, then search by closeness of meaning.

Prompt Engineering in One Slide

  • A prompt is the input you give a model: an instruction plus any context or examples
  • Prompt engineering is crafting prompts to get better answers
  • No retraining is needed; you change the words
  • Prompts can set a role, a format and limits
  • Module 8 covers techniques such as zero-shot, few-shot and chain-of-thought

Exam tip: Changing the prompt is the cheapest way to change a model's behavior.

Use Cases for Generative AI

Use case Example at Cedar and Salt
Image, video and audio generation Draft marketing images for a new destination
Summarization Short summaries of long guest reviews
AI assistants A trip-planning helper
Translation Listings in many languages
Code generation Helping engineers write code
Customer service agents Handling booking changes
Search Finding policy answers by meaning
Recommendation engines Trip ideas written in a traveler's style

Exam tip: Generating, summarizing or translating content is a generative AI use case.

The Foundation Model Lifecycle

  • Data selection: choose and prepare broad data
  • Model selection: pick the base model that fits
  • Pre-training: train on huge data; builders do this, not most users
  • Fine-tuning: adapt to your task or domain
  • Evaluation, deployment and feedback, then improve and repeat

Exam tip: Pre-training comes first and is huge; fine-tuning comes after and is smaller.

Token-Based Pricing [Verify live]

  • On Amazon Bedrock, on-demand pricing is per token: a price for input tokens and one for output tokens
  • Longer prompts and longer answers cost more and take longer
  • Batch inference is discounted for some models, about 50% lower
  • Provisioned Throughput buys capacity per model unit for a commitment term; it suits steady, high volume
  • Custom models add training, storage and inference charges
  • As of 5 November 2026: details are on the Amazon Bedrock pricing page

Exam tip: Variable use: pay per token. Steady, heavy use: consider provisioned throughput.

Context Engineering [Verify live]

  • A model sees only what is in its context window; it keeps no memory by itself
  • Context engineering is deciding what goes into that window: instructions, retrieved documents, conversation history, memory and tool results
  • Better context gives better answers; too much context raises cost and latency
  • Agents add short-term memory for a session and long-term memory across sessions
  • As of 5 November 2026: AWS has no single definition page; this is the practice as its posts and documentation describe it

Exam tip: Right information, in the right amount, at the right time: that is context engineering.

3Agents, MCP and practice

Agentic AI: Core Ideas

  • An AI agent uses an FM to reason about a goal and act on it
  • Tool usage: the agent calls tools, such as search, databases and APIs
  • Memory management: it keeps context within a session and across sessions
  • Workflow orchestration: it plans steps, runs them and adapts
  • A single agent handles one job; a multi-agent system splits a complex job among specialist agents

Exam tip: Reasoning, tools, memory and orchestration are the building blocks of an agent.

Multi-Agent Patterns

Pattern How it works
Agents as tools A supervisor agent hands sub-tasks to specialist agents, as if calling tools
Workflow A fixed sequence of steps, each run by an agent
Graph Agents are nodes and the edges decide the path
Swarm Agents hand off work to one another as it unfolds
  • Agents talk to each other through communication patterns and open protocols such as A2A (agent to agent)

Exam tip: One coordinator with specialists: agents as tools. Fixed steps: workflow.

Model Context Protocol (MCP) [Verify live]

  • MCP is an open standard for connecting AI agents and models to external tools and data
  • It is often compared to a "USB-C for AI applications": one standard plug
  • An MCP server exposes tools, resources and prompts; an MCP client in the agent connects to it
  • AgentCore Gateway can turn APIs and Lambda functions into MCP tools
  • As of 5 November 2026: see the AWS Prescriptive Guidance pages on agentic protocols

Exam tip: MCP's role: one standard way to connect agents to external systems.

What the Exam Asks: GenAI Core Concepts

  • Which term: token, chunk, embedding, vector, FM, LLM, transformer, multi-modal or diffusion
  • Which use case: generate, summarize, assist, translate, code, serve or search
  • Which lifecycle step: pre-training, fine-tuning, evaluation or deployment
  • Which cost driver: input and output tokens, batch, provisioned throughput
  • Which agent idea: tools, memory, orchestration, a multi-agent pattern or MCP

Exam tip: Name the idea in plain words first, then match it to the term.

Design Check: Cedar and Salt's GenAI Vocabulary

Cedar and Salt needs to Concept
Find review passages similar in meaning to a question Embeddings in a vector index
Split long policy PDFs into pieces before indexing Chunking
Predict the bill for a month of chats Input and output tokens
Let a supervisor hand work to a flights agent and a hotels agent Multi-agent (agents as tools)
Let agents call external tools the same way MCP
Order the lifecycle: data, model, pre-train, fine-tune, evaluate, deploy, feedback FM lifecycle
  • Cover the right column, answer each row yourself, then compare

4Exam Q&A

4.1 Practice questions (choose the best answer; some ask for two)

S1Which statement best describes a foundation model?

  • AA small model trained on labeled data for exactly one narrow task
  • BA large model pre-trained on broad, unlabeled data and adapted to many tasks
  • CA hand-written rule engine that was coded for one specific workflow only
  • DA database that stores documents as embeddings so they can be searched
Show the answer

Answer: B. A foundation model is a very large deep learning model pre-trained on broad, unlabeled data, so one model can handle many tasks when prompted or adapted. A single-task model, a rule engine and a vector database are different things.

S2Cedar and Salt wants to find guest-review passages that are close in meaning to a traveler's question, even when they share no exact words. What makes this possible?

  • ACounting how often each exact word appears in the question and the reviews
  • BTranslating every review into a single language before searching for matches
  • CSorting all of the reviews alphabetically so that similar ones sit together
  • DEmbeddings stored as vectors, compared by closeness of meaning
Show the answer

Answer: D. Embeddings turn text into vectors in which similar meanings are close together, so a question can be matched to passages by meaning. Word counts, translation and sorting do not capture meaning.

S3Which TWO things affect the cost of a call to a foundation model that is billed per token? (Select TWO.)

  • AThe number of tokens in the prompt
  • BThe color theme of the application
  • CThe number of tokens in the generated response
  • DThe font used in the prompt
  • EThe number of users who read the answer
Show the answer

Answer: A, C. On-demand token pricing charges for input tokens, which come from the prompt, and for output tokens, which come from the response. Presentation choices and the number of readers do not change the token count.

S4Which kind of model generates an image by learning to remove noise step by step?

  • AA diffusion model
  • BA recommender model
  • CA clustering model
  • DA speech recognition model
Show the answer

Answer: A. Diffusion models are trained by adding noise to images and learning to reverse the process, so they can create a clear image from noise, often steered by a text prompt.

S5Which sequence lists the foundation model lifecycle in the correct order?

  • AEvaluation, pre-training, data selection, deployment, fine-tuning, model selection, feedback
  • BDeployment, evaluation, model selection, pre-training, data selection, fine-tuning, feedback
  • CData selection, model selection, pre-training, fine-tuning, evaluation, deployment, feedback
  • DFine-tuning, data selection, deployment, pre-training, feedback, evaluation, model selection
Show the answer

Answer: C. The lifecycle runs from data selection and model selection through pre-training and fine-tuning, then evaluation, deployment and feedback, which leads back to earlier steps.

S6What is the role of the Model Context Protocol (MCP) in agentic applications?

  • AIt trains foundation models on large sets of labeled examples for each task
  • BIt is an open standard for connecting agents to external tools and data
  • CIt compresses prompts into fewer tokens so that every call costs less money
  • DIt stores embeddings in a vector database for fast similarity search
Show the answer

Answer: B. MCP is an open standard that lets agents and models connect to external tools, resources and data in a uniform way. It is not a training method, a compression method or a vector store.

S7Cedar and Salt builds a trip-planning system in which a supervisor agent hands flight searches to one specialist agent and hotel searches to another, then combines their results. Which pattern is this?

  • AA single agent that has no tools and no specialist helpers
  • BA fixed batch inference job that scores a whole dataset overnight
  • CA multi-agent system using agents as tools
  • DA diffusion model that creates images by adding and removing noise
Show the answer

Answer: C. A supervisor that delegates sub-tasks to specialist agents and merges their answers is a multi-agent pattern, often called agents as tools. A single agent with no tools, a batch job and a diffusion model do not describe it.
